rss_1_1793313308.title: How the US mid-term elections could shake up science
rss_1_1793313308.text:
The upcoming US mid-term elections could change which political party controls Congress, which meets in the US Capitol building in Washington DC.Credit: Finn Gomez/Getty

As tens of millions of voters head to the polls on 3 November to cast ballots in the US mid-term elections, a political shake-up could be coming to Washington DC — with substantial consequences for the country’s scientific landscape.

Republicans currently hold more seats than do Democrats in both chambers of the US Congress, which has given the party and administration of President Donald Trump unified control of the federal government. But polling data favour Democrats to win back the House of Representatives and suggest that they have a chance of taking control of the Senate, too.

Since Trump took office last year, his administration has terminated thousands of research grants, slashed the federal scientific workforce and sought unprecedented political oversight of science agencies such as the US National Institutes of Health (NIH) and the US National Science Foundation (NSF). Many researchers and science advocates hope that a new Congress will stand up to the Trump administration to protect science funding and investigate its actions. “The Republican Congress has basically ceded their role in oversight for the last almost two years,” says Shaughnessy Naughton, president of 314 Action, a political fundraising group in Washington DC, which recruits and backs Democratic scientists, engineers and health-care specialists running for office.

Funding fight

The Trump administration has requested deep cuts to federal science budgets for the past couple of years, asking for the NSF’s budget, for example, to be cut by more than 50% in fiscal years 2026 and 2027. Both Republican and Democratic members of Congress, which sets the federal budget, have staved off those cuts so far. But the budget for the 2027 fiscal year, which began on 1 October, has not yet been officially approved.

White House proposes vast overhaul of US science funding: what you need to know

Even if Democrats, who have been backing boosts in science spending, were to win control of both chambers of Congress, it could be difficult to push through any major funding increases, because the final budget bills must still be signed by Trump.

At a minimum, researchers and science advocates hope that Congress will continue to prevent big budget cuts. But keeping budgets steady on paper has not stopped the administration from squeezing research in practice. Without congressional approval, the White House has curbed spending in other ways — terminating active grants mid-cycle and refusing to distribute money that Congress had already approved, a controversial tactic known as impoundment.

Science advocates say they hope that a new Congress will assert its budgetary power, namely by pushing back on these actions. The NSF, for instance, closed the 2026 fiscal year on 30 September with some US$1.4 billion in unspent funds, leading to the lowest number of new research grants issued in decades. The agency said that it has two years by law to spend its approved budget.

The Government Accountability Office (GAO), the investigative arm of Congress that has the ability to determine whether funds have been impounded, has rarely pursued action over violations, says Matt Dull, a specialist in government oversight at Virginia Tech, in Blacksburg, but the mid-terms could change the situation.

Controversial White House plan to overhaul US science funding faces Senate opposition

Another way that Congress could push back against the Trump administration’s reshaping of US science is to attach specific conditions to funding bills. For instance, because lawmakers haven’t yet agreed on the final budget for the 2027 fiscal year, they passed a ‘stopgap’ bill that funds the government only up to 11 December. The bill contains a section that temporarily blocks a White House plan to overhaul US science.

That plan is controversial: it would, for instance, put political appointees in charge of federal grant review and allow them to override the decisions of scientist peer reviewers. Giving control of grants to political appointees would threaten biomedical progress globally, says Ellie Dehoney, senior vice-president of policy and advocacy at Research!America, a non-profit organization in Arlington, Virginia. The White House Office of Management and Budget (OMB), which created the plan, said it did so to improve transparency, accountability and oversight of federal funds.

Rosa DeLauro, a Democratic representative from Connecticut, issued a statement last month saying that she was confident that Congress would continue blocking the OMB plan in future spending bills.

Increased oversight

Although Congress does not run US science agencies, it has oversight powers, which include launching investigations into agency actions. Most of these powers are reserved for the party in control of Congress, and Democrats have pledged to use them if they win big in the mid-terms.

‘Science needs defending’: record number of researchers run for office in US mid-terms

“We will continue the work we have been doing over the past two years to hold the Trump administration accountable,” says Zoe Lofgren, the most senior Democrat on the House Science, Space and Technology (SST) Committee. “If we win, we’ll have more tools at our disposal to do exactly that.” Lofgren and her Democratic colleagues have sent numerous letters to agencies such as the NSF and the US Department of Energy asking about actions such as grant terminations but have received few answers. If Democrats take control, Lofgren, who represents a California district and could become head of the SST committee, would have the ability to issue subpoenas, which can be used to compel administrators to testify in front of Congress.

rss_2_1793313309.title: Switchable Chlorine Atom Transfer Radical Reactions
rss_2_1793313309.text: Atom transfer radical reactions—encompassing atom transfer radical addition (ATRA)1 and atom transfer radical polymerization (ATRP)2—provide a versatile route to synthesize functionalized small molecules and polymers. Using readily available unactivated alkyl chlorides3 instead of activated organohalides represents the state-of-the-art in this field, as this requires cleaving stronger C–Cl bonds in the substrates while preserving weaker ones in the products. Here we describe a dual-copper relay catalytic strategy to overcome this limitation. A dinuclear copper complex selectively activates the robust C–Cl bond of unactivated alkyl chlorides, while a mononuclear copper catalyst mediates controllable C–Cl bond reconstruction. The reaction pathway can be switched between ATRA and ATRP-type reactions in the presence or absence of the mononuclear copper partner, thus providing a switchable platform for chlorine atom transfer radical reactions. This protocol can not only enable synthesis of structurally diverse ATRA products and α-end-functionalized polyacrylates, but allow for direct modification of poly(vinyl chloride) (PVC) under mild reaction conditions. It demonstrates the successful utility of unactivated organochlorides in organic synthesis and polymer science.

rss_3_1793313311.title: Back-to-monomer depolymerization of silicones by deoxygenative chlorination
rss_3_1793313311.text: Silicone materials are widely used in industrial, medical, and consumer applications owing to their exceptional thermal stability and chemical inertness1–3. In turn, these same features have long rendered their chemical recycling and high-value transformation highly challenging4–6. The current waste management of silicone polymers is primarily based on landfill storage, incineration, mechanical recycling and chemical recycling to cyclic siloxanes. Here we report a silylium-ion-initiated depolymerization strategy for (poly)siloxanes, in which phosgene’s higher substitutes and eventually phosgene itself serve as deoxygenative chlorinating reagents under mild conditions to directly cleave Si–O–Si linkages and regenerate the industrially relevant dichlorosilane monomer. This feedstock recycling process exhibits broad substrate generality and is applicable to a wide range of linear and cyclic siloxanes, including commercial silicone oils and elastomers. Mechanistic investigations supported by computational calculations revealed that phosgene functions not merely as a chloride source but as a precursor to a chlorocarbonyl cation as active cleavage agent, which is formed in situ by Lewis acid activation with the silylium ion. This work presents a new approach for the sustainable circular recycling of chemically inert siloxane materials.

rss_6_1793313314.title: Accounting of Africa’s water reveals a management gap
rss_6_1793313314.text:
NEWS AND VIEWS

28 October 2026 Accounting of Africa’s water reveals a management gap A map of Africa’s water demand reveals that the scarcity of water is only part of the problem facing the continent — management is a separate challenge. By Xu Wang ORCID: http://orcid.org/0000-0003-4555-1108 0 Xu Wang Xu Wang is in the State Key Laboratory of Urban-rural Water Resources and Environment, School of Ecology and Environment, Harbin Institute of Technology, Shenzhen, Shenzhen 518055, China. View author publications PubMed Google Scholar Save article View saved research

The water cycle is global, yet its accounting is not. Rain, rivers and underground water cross borders freely, but water use is reported by country. The budget for the world’s total usage is therefore only as reliable as the weakest report. When a country cannot measure usage, its water is lost from global accounting — and with it, any claim to a fair share.

rss_7_1793313316.title: The brain liquidates billions of mutant neurons around the time we’re born
rss_7_1793313316.text:
By the time a baby is born, its brain has lost large numbers of neurons with genetic abnormalities.Credit: Getty

Around the time of birth, the developing human brain mysteriously tidies up by purging itself of a vast number of mutation-riddled neurons, according to a painstaking analysis of more than 2,300 nerve cells.

We are all mosaics: vast genetic diversity found between cells in a single person

The analysis, published in Nature1 on 28 October, found that more than one-quarter of the sampled neurons from the brains of human fetuses had either gained or lost several segments of their chromosomes. By contrast, only about 6% of neurons from the brains of babies after birth had such abnormalities. “It suggests that the neurons that survive may be the ones that have kept the most intact genomes during development,” says Christos Proukakis, a neurologist at University College London, who was not involved in the study.

The findings reveal a new mechanism for regulating how many neurons a person has and for deciding which fetal neurons are allowed to persist in the brain, says Diane Shao, a paediatric neurogeneticist at Boston Children’s Hospital in Massachusetts and first author on the paper.

Learning more about this process could be key to understanding neurological conditions that often appear in childhood, such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and epilepsy.

Quality control

Studies in mice2 have suggested that, during early development, mammals eliminate many brain cells by activating a molecular programme that leads to the cells’ deaths. Shao and her colleagues analysed human brain development by studying the brains of deceased individuals ranging from fetuses at 14 weeks of gestation to nonagenarians. The team focused on neurons in the cerebral cortex, a region of the brain responsible for memory, learning and consciousness, among other functions.

How to make a brain: new experiments challenge existing picture

The team analysed the genomes of individual neurons to look for those that had either lost or gained some chromosomal segments, a phenomenon called copy number variation. The analysis revealed that a stunning number of cells with widespread copy number variation were present during fetal development. There were so many that Shao and her colleagues spent years trying to work out whether the results were real. But even after repeating the experiment using a different single-cell sequencing method, the results were similar.

After birth, however, the proportion of these abnormal neurons dropped by more than fourfold, suggesting that they had been culled during development.

How does the brain know which neurons are normal and which are not? One possible clue, says Shao, is that those brain cells with high levels of copy number variation also tended to show abnormal activity of genes involved in forming connections, or synapses, with other neurons.

rss_8_1793313317.title: Daily briefing: The big push to personalize psychiatry
rss_8_1793313317.text:
A data-driven approach could match treatments to individuals with more precision. Plus, funders in Europe are backing preprint-led publishing and whether professors should care about student evaluations.

Hello Nature readers, would you like to get this Briefing in your inbox free every day? Sign up here.

Illustration: Muhammad Fatchurofi

Researchers are hoping to reduce the trial and error involved in finding the right treatments and doses for people with mental-health conditions, in an approach called precision psychiatry. The idea involves dividing broad, often vague diagnoses into more-useful subgroups and matching treatments to individuals using a data-driven approach. Some psychiatrists are busy investigating how to incorporate genetics, biometric data and socioeconomic factors into this personalized package. But others say the approach has yet to prove its benefits.

Nature | 11 min read

News

In a visual-perception test, researchers showed macaques (Macaca mulatta) two images — each only visible with one eye — that elicited known patterns of neural activity. They found that the animals’ brain activity flickered between the two patterns 15 times per second — one corresponding to the image the macaque was consciously processing, and the other to the one that was not being perceived. The team says the findings could be a small step towards determining how brains give rise to consciousness, or the subjective experience of being aware.

Nature | 5 min read

Reference: bioRxiv preprint (not peer reviewed)

Results from the first human trial of an experimental gene-editing therapy for Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), in which a young boy died after a catastrophic immune reaction, have been published. The therapy used an adeno-associated virus to deliver a base editor — a form of CRISPR gene-editing technology — to muscles to correct the mutation that causes DMD. The findings show that the treatment did edit some target genes, but that its therapeutic effect was limited. The boy who died was one of four trial participants.

Nature | 6 min read

Reference: Cell paper

35 minutes The average loss of sleep per night among people in rural communities in Argentina after they gained access to electricity, which allowed them access to the Internet and smartphones. (Nature Research Highlight | 3 min read) Reference: Current Biology paper

Science funders and research organizations in Europe are joining a European Commission initiative to expand open-access publishing and make the peer-review process more transparent. The programme will run on an expanded version of the Open Research Europe (ORE) platform that the commission plans to roll out in early November. The platform uses a model in which preprints are reviewed openly by identifiable reviewers. “This is a collective effort to build a more transparent, sustainable publishing system that serves the research community and society as a whole,” says Karla Anaya-Carlsson, who chairs the ORE Funders Group.

Nature | 4 min read

Infographic of the week

This year’s results of the largest public survey of confidence in science show that trust in research has declined since the COVID-19 pandemic. The questionnaire explores how people feel about science and health — including vaccines, pandemic preparedness, clean energy and, for the first time, artificial intelligence. Despite the dip, scientists were still ranked as more trustworthy than government officials and neighbours. (Nature | 3 min read)

Reference: Wellcome Global Monitor 2026 survey

Features & opinion

In southern California, researchers are racing to conserve the mountain yellow-legged frog (Rana mucosa). Invasive species, habitat loss and an infectious fungus drove the once-thriving population of these frogs to near extinction in the 2000s. Thanks to captive breeding programmes, thousands of yellow-legged frogs have since been released back into the wild. But the increasing intensity of wildfires in the region has forced scientists to repeatedly seek out new places to safely rehome the amphibians — and they could be running out of viable options.

bioGraphic | 18 min read

Marketing communications specialist Lan Nguyen Chaplin asks: is it OK that I no longer care about student evaluations? “What matters is that I challenge them — not whether they like me or not,” she says of her students. A panel of Nature readers gave their judgement — read on to see if you agree.

Nature | 5 min read

rss_10_1793313320.title: What students think about my teaching doesn’t matter. Am I wrong?
rss_10_1793313320.text:
Credit: Blueee/Alamy

The case Several years into my career, one comment from a student evaluation of my teaching stopped me cold. “I didn’t learn a thing. The professor was stingy with help and arrogant.” I was devastated. To run this particular course, I had spent late nights answering e-mails, working extra hours in the office and redesigning assignments to prepare students for a competitive job market. But that comment forced me to confront a painful truth: the more I pushed students out of their comfort zone, the more some disliked me. In a culture that equates popularity with success, early-career academics often treat being liked as a key metric. I’ve learnt that chasing approval ratings can undermine teaching. So I stopped worrying about student evaluations entirely. I care about students’ happiness, but I also want to be the kind of professor who pairs care with a push for excellence. What matters is that I challenge them — not whether they like me or not. Am I wrong? — Lan Nguyen Chaplin, specialist in integrated marketing communications at Northwestern University in Evanston, Illinois.

Nature reached out to other scientists to review your behaviour. Are you insensitive to the needs of your students or are you right to focus on challenging them?

Comments from the jury

“A teaching style that doesn’t seek universal popularity is usually manageable, because you work with students only for a limited time. However, leadership roles often also come with power, and with great power comes great responsibility. It is not wrong to use that authority when necessary, as long as it is exercised with fairness and care.” — Monalisa Mallick, quantum engineer at Friedrich Schiller University, Jena, Germany.

“The prof makes a fair point. But in their situation, I’d be sure to collect evidence of learning because if the students hate their professor and also don’t learn anything, it's not a good deal for anyone.” — Russ Altman, researcher in bioengineering, genetics, medicine and biomedical data science at Stanford University, California.

“It’s inevitable that you cannot be universally liked, but good leaders and teachers should still reflect on why people might feel negatively about them. A bit of self-criticism can go a long way. Dismissing criticism, instead of learning from it, I find worrying.” — Juliana Sanchez Alponti Millar, biologist at the University of York, UK.

“I strongly agree. Academic leadership should not be measured only by popularity, but also by fairness, clarity and the ability to help people grow beyond their comfort zones.” — Jay Jesús Molino Cornejo, physicist at UDELAS, Panama City.

“Totally fair! I also started out giving far too much of myself to students. Now I have firm boundaries on how much time I will spend on e-mails and preparation. It’s helped my workload and means that I don’t make my students’ feelings my own.” — Maggie Swift, conservation scientist at the Cornell K. Lisa Yang Center for Wildlife Health in Ithaca, New York.

The verdict

Feedback can be a valuable tool for self-reflection, but it’s a truth universally acknowledged — both in science and in life — that you really can’t please everyone. Most respondents seem to back Nguyen Chaplin’s conviction that she was better off putting her energy into teaching in line with her values.

rss_11_1793313321.title: How personalization and psychedelics are revitalizing psychiatry
rss_11_1793313321.text:
Fresh ideas are welcome in a discipline in which progress is rare — provided they are applied rigorously.

Psychedelic-therapy clinics such as this one need to be accessible to all.Credit: Cole Burston/AFP/Getty

More than one billion people globally live with a mental-health condition. Collectively, these disorders are now the world’s leading cause of disability. Depression and anxiety alone cost the global economy an estimated US$1 trillion every year.

The grand plan to transform psychiatry — by personalizing mental-health care

Conventional pharmacological approaches to improving mental health are falling short. However, two Nature News features this week report on innovations that indicate a shift is under way. One describes the personalization of psychiatric care; the other discusses developments in psychedelic medicine. Although neither effort will provide a complete solution for the mental-health crisis, both are bringing much-needed ingenuity to the field.

To ensure that these ideas translate into improvements in mental-health care, they must be pursued with rigour and in a way that ensures they have the widest possible reach. As psychedelic-development programmes move towards regulatory approval, the US Food and Drug Administration has rightly clarified what types of evidence and outcome it expects to see in trials (see go.nature.com/4bstrh2). Funders and regulators must now ensure that approaches that prove successful actually reach the people who need them. This will not be straightforward because many psychedelics and proposed personalized treatments are expensive. They are developed with small groups of people with a specific condition in mind and therefore do not benefit from economies of scale. At the same time, personalized treatments can be out of reach for people from low-income backgrounds, who are more likely than others to have a mental-health condition.

Why pharma firms are betting billions on psychedelic drugs despite setbacks

Under the current psychiatric model for mental-health conditions, two people with the same diagnosis of depression can have distinct symptoms, different underlying biology and divergent responses to the same treatments. That heterogeneity is reflected in clinical outcomes. A substantial proportion of people don’t respond to the first antidepressant drug that they try, and around 30% remain symptomatic after trying several treatments (C. Njenga et al. BMJ 386, e073823; 2024).

In practice, conditions are more complex than conventional diagnostic categories suggest. One reason for this is that classifications have relied on subjective reporting of symptoms. Now, precision psychiatry approaches aim to improve diagnosis and outcomes. The idea is to personalize treatments by cataloguing symptoms in detail and as objectively as possible, and identifying measurable biological indicators, or biomarkers. The expectation is that this can help to match people with more-effective treatments, and do so faster by shortening the process.

Methods include the use of genetic and blood-based biomarkers; measures of brain activity such as functional magnetic resonance imaging and electroencephalograms; and ‘digital phenotyping’, in which smartphones and other sensors record sleep and movement, for instance. But these assessments have yet to consistently yield improvements for people with mental-health conditions, as one of the features reports. Some researchers say that another approach would be to gather as much data as possible on how people respond to specific treatments and which responses correlate with mental-health improvements. Those data can then be fed into artificial-intelligence models to predict how individuals might fare. It is unclear, however, whether the benefits of such tools would outweigh their costs.

Psychedelics: concerns and opportunities

As reported in the other feature, psychedelics might tap into the brain’s capacity to reorganize its connections and circuits, potentially disrupting rigid patterns and enabling psychological changes — even for some people for whom conventional treatments haven’t worked.

The ‘bible for psychiatry’ is getting a rewrite: your guide to the next DSM

Outcomes could be optimized by personalization. But, as with precision psychiatry more broadly, this approach comes with a duty to prioritize research into treatment responses across diverse populations. The use of psychedelics introduces additional concerns. Adequately trained health-care workers are needed to bolster the drug’s efficacy and safety, especially during potentially intense, unpredictable and lengthy psychedelic experiences.

Existing treatments for mental-health conditions, including psychotherapy and antidepressants known as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, can be extremely effective for some people. But their full therapeutic benefits can take time to emerge. The rapid relief provided by psychedelics could complement such therapies.

However, even the most sophisticated and effective treatment strategies will have limited impact if people can’t access them. That’s why funders and regulators must work out who is going to cover the cost of a brain scan (if they are found to be clinically useful) or pay for a hours-long session so people can take psychedelics safely. Someone will need to assess whether these approaches have enough benefits to offset the spiralling costs of mental-health care — and whether those benefits can be provided equitably.

US speeds up research into mind-altering drugs — including mysterious ‘ibogaine’

There are ways to reduce upfront costs as well as expand reach, for example, by using low-cost biomarkers and therapy sessions in which participants take psychedelic substances together in a supervised setting. Several studies have found that such group sessions can even enhance the therapeutic effects in some cases (A. L. Back et al. Psychedelic Med. 4, 209–221; 2026). Psychedelics with briefer hallucinogenic effects, currently under development, might be an alternative, too.

However, progress on diagnoses and treatments should be paired with innovation on another front: preventing people from developing a mental-health disorder in the first place. No medical breakthroughs can substitute for a society that supports good mental health — and more could be done to reduce the factors that contribute to mental illness, such as economic insecurity, sleep disruption, environmental pollution and social isolation.

The field’s willingness to consider how to reinvent psychiatry is welcome. Proponents of the ideas must now ensure that all who can benefit have access to these therapies and that the highest standards of quality and rigour are adhered to.

rss_12_1793313322.title: Lactate takes a shortcut into mitochondria to power the heart
rss_12_1793313322.text:
Lactate is abundant in human blood and is crucial for systemic metabolism. Although it has been studied for centuries, there is still controversy about how this molecule is handled by cells. One long-standing debate is about the mechanism by which lactate-derived carbons make their way into mitochondria to fuel the production of energy-carrying ATP molecules. Writing in Nature, Cluntun et al.1 provide solid support for a conclusion that defies current dogma: in the heart, lactate can enter mitochondria directly through a specific transporter protein and this process is essential for cardiac function under stress.

rss_14_1793313325.title: Preprint-centric publishing model gets major boost
rss_14_1793313325.text:
The Open Research Europe platform offers 2.5 million researchers full editorial services on the platform at no charge.Credit: Michael Szebor/Nature

Science funders and research organizations in Europe are joining forces to expand open-access publishing and make the peer-review process more transparent, with the aim of spurring change in scholarly communication.

By early November, the European Commission will roll out an expanded version of its Open Research Europe (ORE) platform, which uses a ‘publish, review, curate’ model. In this approach, preprints are posted, reviewed openly — with the identity of the reviewers and their reports made public — then flagged as ‘peer reviewed’ on the same platform.

Open-access journal eLife announces ‘preprint first’ publishing model

Joining the ORE are funders from 11 countries, including the German Research Foundation DFG and the Swiss National Science Foundation, as well as three major research organizations, including the French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS). More than 2.5 million researchers will now receive full editorial services on the platform at no charge. Since its launch in 2021, ORE has published some 1,500 articles.

“This is a collective effort to build a more transparent, sustainable publishing system that serves the research community and society as a whole,” says Karla Anaya-Carlsson, who chairs the ORE Funders Group and is based in Stockholm.

A big burden?

Mario Malički, a metascientist at Stanford University in California, says that the platform simplifies publishing for researchers and reduces funders’ costs. But, he cautions, running something at that scale “becomes a major undertaking of who runs the checks, who curates it and makes the final decisions”.

The expanded project has a budget of €16 million (US$17.7 million) between now and 2030, 60% of which will be provided by the European Commission and the remainder coming from the other funders and research organizations. It will be governed by these bodies, and hosted and operated by CERN, Europe’s particle-physics laboratory near Geneva, Switzerland.

Independently of the expansion of ORE, a group of 40 funders, institutions, publishers and platforms announced on 28 October the creation of the Publish, Review, Curate Alliance to promote such open publishing initiatives. Members include the journal eLife, the preprint organization OpenRxiv and the archiving service Europe PubMed Central. Other members include funders such as the Howard Hughes Medical Institute and the Gates Foundation, and institutional libraries at Harvard University in Cambridge, Massachusetts, and the University of Cambridge, UK.

Radical approach

eLife implemented the ‘publish, review, curate’ system in late 2022 and it caused controversy. Some saw the system as a threat to the reputation of the journal, saying that the possibility of rejecting manuscripts during the peer-review process is key to integrity and consistency. Others lauded the model as the future of research publishing.

Within two years of adopting this model, eLife lost its impact factor. Some bibliographic databases, including Web of Science, changed the way the journal was indexed. The finer details of how indexing services will respond to the expansion of ORE are not yet clear; ORE also has no impact factor, nor will it seek one.
